points.en: The believer lives in two kingdoms: render to Caesar what is Caesar's and to God what is God's, owing governing authorities real obedience.
That obedience is never absolute: when the state commands what God forbids or forbids what God commands, we must obey God rather than men.
The fortress is withdrawal into a Christian bunker, refusing engagement with the world and hiding the light.
The chameleon blends so completely into the culture that the church becomes indistinguishable from the world.
Scripture's answer (Romans 12:2) is to be transformed by a renewed mind and engage the culture with discernment, neither fleeing it nor conforming to it.
'Judge not' forbids hypocritical, censorious, self-righteous judgment, not all moral discernment.
Self-examination comes first (remove the plank from your own eye), and then the church is commanded to judge rightly, including those inside the church.
Courage and humility must be held together: discernment without self-examination becomes Pharisaism, and self-examination without discernment becomes cowardice.
The first purpose of all church discipline is the restoration of the sinner, never his destruction.
In 2 Corinthians 2 the church must forgive, comfort and reaffirm love to the repentant man, lest he be swallowed up with sorrow.
Refusing to forgive the repentant gives Satan an advantage over the church (2 Corinthians 2:11).
Godly sorrow produces real repentance and a turning, while the sorrow of the world is mere regret at being caught.
Wise restoration is neither rushed nor refused: a fallen leader restored before repentance is tested wounds the church and himself, but refusing a penitent is cruelty.
It often follows a clear written path with defined steps, proven faithfulness, gradual reintegration and ongoing care.
Christian ethics is never a ladder to earn God's favor but the fruit of a favor already given: grace first, then the holy life it produces.
Each duty studied is what gratitude looks like in practice, and the minister should write a personal Pastoral Ethics Statement and keep watchful, since no one falls all at once but drifts.
The rich man's sin was neglect: he stepped over Lazarus at his gate day after day and did nothing.
After death the roles were reversed: he saw, too late, the beggar comforted, so we will all give account one day.
A pastor should therefore see and spend himself on the person God sets before him now (the poor, the fallen, the wounded, his own family).
The course ends with Paul's testimony: 'I have fought the good fight, I have finished the race, I have kept the faith' (2 Timothy 4:7).
The goal is not to begin well, be admired or avoid scandal, but to finish as a faithful, holy shepherd of the flock Christ bought with His blood.
Obedience to the state is real but not absolute, because Caesar himself belongs to God.
When the state commands what God forbids or forbids what God commands, the believer obeys God rather than men, keeping the conscience that belongs to God alone.
Otherwise the believer is to be the best of citizens, honoring the magistrate and subject to authorities ordained by God (Romans 13:1).
Discernment: judge rightly with self-examination first, avoiding both Pharisaism and cowardice.
Restoration: the aim of discipline is the penitent's restoration, neither rushed nor refused.
Capstone: ethics is the fruit of grace not a ladder, and the pastor must watch against drift and finish faithfully, knowing he will give account.
